questions.q: A motor rotates with a uniform angular acceleration. It completes $40$ revolutions in $5$ s. If its initial angular speed is $300$ rpm, what is its final angular speed in rpm?
questions.question: A motor rotates with a uniform angular acceleration. It completes $40$ revolutions in $5$ s. If its initial angular speed is $300$ rpm, what is its final angular speed in rpm?
questions.solution:
Initial angular speed, $\omega_0 = 300$ rpm = $\dfrac{300 \times 2\pi}{60} = 10\pi$ rad/s

Angular displacement, $\theta = 40$ revolutions = $40 \times 2\pi = 80\pi$ rad

Using the equation of kinematics for rotational motion:
$\theta = \omega_0 t + \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2$
$80\pi = 10\pi \times 5 + \dfrac{1}{2} \alpha (5)^2$
$80\pi = 50\pi + 12.5 \alpha$
$\alpha = \dfrac{30\pi}{12.5} = 2.4\pi$ rad/s$^2$

Final angular speed, $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$
$\omega = 10\pi + 2.4\pi \times 5 = 22\pi$ rad/s

Converting back to rpm:
Final angular speed = $\dfrac{22\pi \times 60}{2\pi} = 660$ rpm

Answer: $660$

questions.q: A uniform solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is rotating freely about its diameter with an angular velocity $\omega_0$. Due to internal forces, the sphere contracts uniformly such that its radius becomes $\dfrac{R}{2}$. What is the work done by the internal forces during this contraction?
questions.question: A uniform solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is rotating freely about its diameter with an angular velocity $\omega_0$. Due to internal forces, the sphere contracts uniformly such that its radius becomes $\dfrac{R}{2}$. What is the work done by the internal forces during this contraction?
questions.solution:
The initial moment of inertia of the solid sphere is $I_i = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$.

When the radius becomes $\dfrac{R}{2}$, the final moment of inertia is $I_f = \dfrac{2}{5}M\left(\dfrac{R}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4} \left(\dfrac{2}{5}MR^2\right) = \dfrac{I_i}{4}$.

Since there is no external torque acting on the sphere, the angular momentum is conserved:
$I_i \omega_0 = I_f \omega_f$
$I_i \omega_0 = \left(\dfrac{I_i}{4}\right) \omega_f \Rightarrow \omega_f = 4\omega_0$

The initial rotational kinetic energy is:
$K_i = \dfrac{1}{2}I_i\omega_0^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{5}MR^2\right)\omega_0^2 = \dfrac{1}{5}MR^2\omega_0^2$

The final rotational kinetic energy is:
$K_f = \dfrac{1}{2}I_f\omega_f^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{I_i}{4}\right)(4\omega_0)^2 = 4 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}I_i\omega_0^2\right) = 4K_i = \dfrac{4}{5}MR^2\omega_0^2$

According to the work-energy theorem, the work done by the internal forces equals the change in rotational kinetic energy:
$W = \Delta K = K_f - K_i = \dfrac{4}{5}MR^2\omega_0^2 - \dfrac{1}{5}MR^2\omega_0^2 = \dfrac{3}{5}MR^2\omega_0^2$

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{5}MR^2\omega_0^2$

Wheel A attains a rotational speed of $600\text{ rpm}$ in $10\text{ s}$, while wheel B attains a rotational speed of $900\text{ rpm}$ in $12\text{ s}$. The ratio of the angular acceleration of wheel A to that of wheel B is
questions.solution:
Let $\alpha_A$ and $\alpha_B$ be the angular accelerations of wheels A and B respectively.

Since both start from rest, the angular acceleration is given by $\alpha = \dfrac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t}$.

For wheel A: $\omega_A = 600\text{ rpm}$, $t_A = 10\text{ s}$.
$\alpha_A \propto \dfrac{600}{10} = 60$

For wheel B: $\omega_B = 900\text{ rpm}$, $t_B = 12\text{ s}$.
$\alpha_B \propto \dfrac{900}{12} = 75$

The ratio of their angular accelerations is:
$\dfrac{\alpha_A}{\alpha_B} = \dfrac{60}{75} = \dfrac{4}{5}$.

The conversion factor from $\text{rpm}$ to $\text{rad s}^{-1}$ cancels out in the ratio.

Answer: $4:5$

questions.question: A car accelerates uniformly such that its speed increases from $36$ km/h to $108$ km/h in $10$ s. If the radius of its wheels is $\dfrac{2}{\pi}$ m, how many revolutions does each wheel complete during this time? Assume no slipping.
questions.solution:
Initial linear speed, $u = 36$ km/h = $36 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 10$ m/s

Final linear speed, $v = 108$ km/h = $108 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 30$ m/s

Distance covered by the car in $t = 10$ s is given by the average velocity multiplied by time:
$s = \left(\dfrac{u + v}{2}\right) t = \left(\dfrac{10 + 30}{2}\right) \times 10 = 200$ m

In pure rolling, the linear distance covered by the center of mass is equal to the distance rolled by the wheel along its circumference.
Circumference of the wheel, $C = 2\pi R = 2\pi \times \dfrac{2}{\pi} = 4$ m

Number of revolutions completed, $N = \dfrac{s}{C} = \dfrac{200}{4} = 50$

Answer: $50$

questions.question: A solid sphere and a thin hollow sphere have the same mass and the same radius. The ratio of the radius of gyration of the solid sphere to that of the hollow sphere, both calculated about an axis tangent to their respective surfaces, is:
questions.solution:
Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia of a solid sphere about a tangent axis is:
$I_{solid} = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2 + MR^2 = \dfrac{7}{5}MR^2$

The radius of gyration of the solid sphere about the tangent is:
$k_{solid} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_{solid}}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{7}{5}}R$

Similarly, the moment of inertia of a thin hollow sphere about a tangent axis is:
$I_{hollow} = \dfrac{2}{3}MR^2 + MR^2 = \dfrac{5}{3}MR^2$

The radius of gyration of the hollow sphere about the tangent is:
$k_{hollow} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_{hollow}}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{5}{3}}R$

The required ratio is:
$\dfrac{k_{solid}}{k_{hollow}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{7/5}R}{\sqrt{5/3}R} = \sqrt{\dfrac{7}{5} \times \dfrac{3}{5}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{21}}{5}$

Thus, the ratio is $\sqrt{21}:5$.

Answer: $\sqrt{21}:5$

questions.q: A uniform solid cylinder of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is rolling without slipping on a flat horizontal surface. Its centre of mass moves with a constant speed $v$. If $L_C$ is the magnitude of its angular momentum about its centre of mass and $L_P$ is the magnitude of its angular momentum about a stationary point $P$ on the ground, the ratio $\dfrac{L_C}{L_P}$ is:
questions.question: A uniform solid cylinder of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is rolling without slipping on a flat horizontal surface. Its centre of mass moves with a constant speed $v$. If $L_C$ is the magnitude of its angular momentum about its centre of mass and $L_P$ is the magnitude of its angular momentum about a stationary point $P$ on the ground, the ratio $\dfrac{L_C}{L_P}$ is:
questions.solution:
For a solid cylinder rolling without slipping, the angular velocity is $\omega = \dfrac{v}{R}$.

The angular momentum about the centre of mass is given by:
$L_C = I_{cm}\omega = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}MR^2\right)\left(\dfrac{v}{R}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}MvR$

The angular momentum about a stationary point $P$ on the ground is the sum of the angular momentum about the centre of mass and the angular momentum of the centre of mass about $P$:
$\vec{L}_P = \vec{L}_C + \vec{r}_{cm} \times M\vec{v}_{cm}$

Since the cylinder is rolling on the ground, the perpendicular distance from $P$ to the line of motion of the centre of mass is $R$. Both the spin and orbital angular momentum vectors point in the same direction.

Thus, the magnitude is:
$L_P = L_C + MvR = \dfrac{1}{2}MvR + MvR = \dfrac{3}{2}MvR$

The required ratio is:
$\dfrac{L_C}{L_P} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}MvR}{\dfrac{3}{2}MvR} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{3}$

questions.q: A uniform solid cylinder of mass $M$, length $L$ and radius $R$ has the same radius of gyration about its central longitudinal axis as it does about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its length. The ratio of its length to its radius $\left(\dfrac{L}{R}\right)$ is:
questions.question: A uniform solid cylinder of mass $M$, length $L$ and radius $R$ has the same radius of gyration about its central longitudinal axis as it does about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its length. The ratio of its length to its radius $\left(\dfrac{L}{R}\right)$ is:
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a uniform solid cylinder of mass $M$, radius $R$ and length $L$ about its central longitudinal axis is:
$I_{1} = \dfrac{MR^2}{2}$
Its radius of gyration about this axis is $k_{1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_{1}}{M}} = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$.

The moment of inertia of the same cylinder about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its length is:
$I_{2} = M\left(\dfrac{R^2}{4} + \dfrac{L^2}{12}\right)$
Its radius of gyration about this axis is $k_{2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{R^2}{4} + \dfrac{L^2}{12}}$.

Given that $k_{1} = k_{2}$, we can equate their squares:
$\dfrac{R^2}{2} = \dfrac{R^2}{4} + \dfrac{L^2}{12}$

$\dfrac{R^2}{2} - \dfrac{R^2}{4} = \dfrac{L^2}{12}$

$\dfrac{R^2}{4} = \dfrac{L^2}{12}$

$3R^2 = L^2$

$\dfrac{L^2}{R^2} = 3 \implies \dfrac{L}{R} = \sqrt{3}$

Answer: $\sqrt{3}$

questions.question: A solid cylinder of mass $4 \mathrm{~kg}$ and radius $0.5 \mathrm{~m}$ is rotating about its axis with an angular speed of $20 \mathrm{~rad/s}$. The work required to bring the cylinder to rest is:
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a solid cylinder about its axis is given by:
$I = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$
$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times (0.5)^2 = 0.5 \mathrm{~kg \cdot m^2}$

According to the work-energy theorem, the work required to stop the cylinder is equal to its initial rotational kinetic energy:
$W = \Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega_0^2$
$W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times (20)^2$
$W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times 400 = 100 \mathrm{~J}$

Using $I = MR^2$ (as for a ring) would incorrectly give $200 \mathrm{~J}$, and omitting the $\dfrac{1}{2}$ factor in kinetic energy would incorrectly give $200 \mathrm{~J}$ or $400 \mathrm{~J}$.

Answer: $100 \mathrm{~J}$

questions.q:
Read the following statements regarding the rotational motion of a system:

(A) If the Earth were to suddenly shrink to half its present radius without any change in mass, the duration of the day would decrease.
(B) The rotational kinetic energy of an isolated collapsing star remains conserved during its contraction.
(C) An ice skater pulling her arms inward decreases her moment of inertia to spin faster.
(D) The angular momentum of an isolated system is conserved only if the net internal force is zero.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.question:
Read the following statements regarding the rotational motion of a system:

(A) If the Earth were to suddenly shrink to half its present radius without any change in mass, the duration of the day would decrease.
(B) The rotational kinetic energy of an isolated collapsing star remains conserved during its contraction.
(C) An ice skater pulling her arms inward decreases her moment of inertia to spin faster.
(D) The angular momentum of an isolated system is conserved only if the net internal force is zero.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Statement (A) is correct. If the Earth shrinks, its moment of inertia $I$ decreases. By conservation of angular momentum ($L = I\omega = \text{constant}$), its angular velocity $\omega$ must increase. Since the time period $T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$, the duration of the day decreases.

Statement (B) is incorrect. For an isolated collapsing star, angular momentum $L$ is conserved, but as it contracts, its moment of inertia $I$ decreases. The rotational kinetic energy is given by $K = \dfrac{L^2}{2I}$. Since $I$ decreases, the kinetic energy increases. It is not conserved.

Statement (C) is correct. Bringing mass closer to the axis of rotation decreases the moment of inertia, which by conservation of angular momentum results in a higher angular velocity (spinning faster).

Statement (D) is incorrect. The angular momentum of a system is conserved if the net external torque is zero. Internal forces do not exert any net torque on the system and thus do not affect the conservation of angular momentum, regardless of whether the net internal force is zero or not.

Therefore, exactly two statements (A and C) are correct.

Answer: Two

questions.q: A uniform circular disc has original mass $M$ and radius $R$. A sector corresponding to an angle of $120^{\circ}$ is removed from it. The radius of gyration of the remaining part of the disc about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is:
questions.question: A uniform circular disc has original mass $M$ and radius $R$. A sector corresponding to an angle of $120^{\circ}$ is removed from it. The radius of gyration of the remaining part of the disc about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is:
questions.solution:
The mass of the remaining part of the disc is $m' = \dfrac{360^{\circ} - 120^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}} M = \dfrac{2}{3} M$.

The moment of inertia of a sector of a disc about its central axis is given by $I = \dfrac{1}{2} (\text{mass of sector}) R^2$.

Thus, the moment of inertia of the remaining part is $I' = \dfrac{1}{2} m' R^2$.

The radius of gyration $k$ is defined using the mass of the actual object, so $I' = m' k^2$.

Equating the two expressions for $I'$:
$m' k^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} m' R^2$

$k^2 = \dfrac{R^2}{2} \Rightarrow k = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$.

Note that the radius of gyration of a sector of a uniform disc is independent of the angle of the sector and is the same as that of a complete disc.

Answer: $\dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.question: A thin circular ring and a solid cylinder have the same mass and the same radius. The ratio of the radius of gyration of the ring about its central axis to the radius of gyration of the solid cylinder about its central axis is:
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a thin circular ring of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about its central axis is $I_{ring} = MR^2$.

The radius of gyration for the ring is $k_{ring} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_{ring}}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{MR^2}{M}} = R$.

The moment of inertia of a solid cylinder of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about its central axis is $I_{cyl} = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$.

The radius of gyration for the solid cylinder is $k_{cyl} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_{cyl}}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{MR^2}{2M}} = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$.

The required ratio is $\dfrac{k_{ring}}{k_{cyl}} = \dfrac{R}{R/\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{1}$, which is $\sqrt{2}:1$.

Answer: $\sqrt{2}:1$

questions.question: A heavy flywheel rotating at $1500\text{ rpm}$ experiences a constant frictional torque. It slows down to $900\text{ rpm}$ in $12\text{ s}$. How much additional time will it take for the flywheel to come to a complete stop?
questions.solution:
Let the constant angular retardation be $\alpha$.

Using the first equation of rotational motion, $\omega = \omega_0 - \alpha t$.

For the first interval:
Initial angular speed, $\omega_0 = 1500\text{ rpm}$
Final angular speed, $\omega = 900\text{ rpm}$
Time, $t = 12\text{ s}$

The rate of decrease of angular speed is:
$\alpha = \dfrac{1500 - 900}{12} = \dfrac{600}{12} = 50\text{ rpm s}^{-1}$.

For the second interval, the flywheel slows down from $900\text{ rpm}$ to rest ($0\text{ rpm}$).
The additional time $t'$ required is:
$t' = \dfrac{900 - 0}{\alpha} = \dfrac{900}{50} = 18\text{ s}$.

Answer: $18\text{ s}$

The ratio $\dfrac{L_P}{L_C}$ is :
questions.question: A uniform solid cylinder of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is rolling without slipping on a flat horizontal surface. Let $L_C$ be the magnitude of its angular momentum about its center of mass, and $L_P$ be the magnitude of its angular momentum about a stationary point on the ground. The ratio $\dfrac{L_P}{L_C}$ is :
questions.solution:
For a uniform solid cylinder rolling without slipping with center of mass velocity $v$, its angular velocity is $\omega = \dfrac{v}{R}$.

The moment of inertia of the solid cylinder about its center of mass is $I_{cm} = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$.

The angular momentum about the center of mass is:
$L_C = I_{cm}\omega = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}MR^2\right)\left(\dfrac{v}{R}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}MvR$

The angular momentum about a stationary point $P$ on the ground is given by:
$\vec{L}_P = \vec{L}_{cm} + \vec{r}_{cm/P} \times M\vec{v}_{cm}$

Since the cylinder is rolling, the direction of $\vec{L}_{cm}$ and the cross product $\vec{r}_{cm/P} \times M\vec{v}_{cm}$ are the same (both point into the plane of motion). The perpendicular distance from $P$ to the line of motion of the center of mass is $R$.

Thus, the magnitude is:
$L_P = L_C + MvR$
$L_P = \dfrac{1}{2}MvR + MvR = \dfrac{3}{2}MvR$

The ratio is:
$\dfrac{L_P}{L_C} = \dfrac{\dfrac{3}{2}MvR}{\dfrac{1}{2}MvR} = 3$

Answer: $3$

questions.question: For a uniform solid cylinder of radius $R$ and length $L$, the radius of gyration about its central geometric axis is equal to its radius of gyration about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its length. The ratio $\dfrac{L}{R}$ is:
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a uniform solid cylinder about its central geometric axis is $I_1 = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$.
Its radius of gyration about this axis is $K_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_1}{M}} = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$.

The moment of inertia of the cylinder about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its length is $I_2 = M\left(\dfrac{R^2}{4} + \dfrac{L^2}{12}\right)$.
Its radius of gyration about this axis is $K_2 = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_2}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{R^2}{4} + \dfrac{L^2}{12}}$.

Given that $K_1 = K_2$, we have:
$K_1^2 = K_2^2$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{R^2}{2} = \dfrac{R^2}{4} + \dfrac{L^2}{12}$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{R^2}{2} - \dfrac{R^2}{4} = \dfrac{L^2}{12}$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{R^2}{4} = \dfrac{L^2}{12}$
$\Rightarrow L^2 = 3R^2$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{L}{R} = \sqrt{3}$

Answer: $\sqrt{3}$

questions.question: A horizontal uniform circular disc of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is rotating with an angular velocity $\omega_0$ about a frictionless vertical axis passing through its centre. Two small point masses, each of mass $m$, are gently placed at diametrically opposite edges of the disc. What will be the final angular velocity of the system?
questions.solution:
The initial moment of inertia of the disc about its central axis is $I_i = \dfrac{MR^2}{2}$.

When two point masses, each of mass $m$, are placed at the edges (distance $R$ from the axis), the final moment of inertia of the system becomes:
$I_f = \dfrac{MR^2}{2} + 2mR^2 = \left(\dfrac{M}{2} + 2m\right)R^2 = \left(\dfrac{M + 4m}{2}\right)R^2$

Since no external torque acts on the system, the angular momentum is conserved:
$I_i \omega_i = I_f \omega_f$

$\left(\dfrac{MR^2}{2}\right) \omega_0 = \left(\dfrac{M + 4m}{2}\right)R^2 \omega_f$

$\omega_f = \dfrac{M}{M + 4m}\omega_0$

Answer: $\dfrac{M}{M + 4m}\omega_0$

questions.question: The ratio of the radius of gyration of a uniform solid sphere about an axis tangent to its surface to the radius of gyration of the sphere about its diameter is
questions.solution:
For a uniform solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$:

Moment of inertia about its diameter is $I_{\text{diameter}} = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$.
Radius of gyration about the diameter, $k_{\text{diameter}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_{\text{diameter}}}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{5}}R$.

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a tangent is $I_{\text{tangent}} = I_{\text{diameter}} + MR^2 = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2 + MR^2 = \dfrac{7}{5}MR^2$.
Radius of gyration about the tangent, $k_{\text{tangent}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_{\text{tangent}}}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{7}{5}}R$.

The required ratio is $\dfrac{k_{\text{tangent}}}{k_{\text{diameter}}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{7/5}R}{\sqrt{2/5}R} = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{2}}$.

Let the initial time period be $T_i$ and the initial radius be $R_i$.
Since the length of the day decreases by $36\%$, the final time period is:
$T_f = T_i - 0.36 T_i = 0.64 T_i$

By conservation of angular momentum, $I_i \omega_i = I_f \omega_f$.
For a uniform solid sphere, $I = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$.
Since $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$, we have $\dfrac{R_i^2}{T_i} = \dfrac{R_f^2}{T_f}$.

$\left(\dfrac{R_f}{R_i}\right)^2 = \dfrac{T_f}{T_i} = 0.64$

Taking the square root on both sides:
$\dfrac{R_f}{R_i} = \sqrt{0.64} = 0.8$

This means the final radius is $80\%$ of the initial radius.
The percentage decrease in the radius is:
$\dfrac{R_i - R_f}{R_i} \times 100\% = (1 - 0.8) \times 100\% = 20\%$

$K' = \sqrt{2}K$.

Final angular speed $\omega = 300 \text{ rpm}$

$\omega = 300 \times \dfrac{2\pi}{60} \text{ rad s}^{-1} = 10\pi \text{ rad s}^{-1}$

Calculate the angular acceleration $\alpha$ using the first equation of rotational kinematics:
$\alpha = \dfrac{\omega - \omega_0}{t} = \dfrac{10\pi - 0}{5} = 2\pi \text{ rad s}^{-2}$

The tangential acceleration $a_t$ is related to angular acceleration by the formula:
$a_t = \alpha R$
$a_t = 2\pi \times 0.4 = 0.8\pi \text{ m s}^{-2}$

Answer: $0.8\pi \text{ m s}^{-2}$

questions.q: A uniform rod of mass $M$ and length $L$ is hinged at one of its ends. It is held in a horizontal position and then released from rest. The angular speed of the rod when it reaches the lowest (vertical) position is:
questions.question: A uniform rod of mass $M$ and length $L$ is hinged at one of its ends. It is held in a horizontal position and then released from rest. The angular speed of the rod when it reaches the lowest (vertical) position is:
questions.solution:
When the rod moves from the horizontal to the vertical position, its center of mass falls by a distance $h = \dfrac{L}{2}$.

The loss in gravitational potential energy is:
$\Delta U = Mg\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)$

This loss in potential energy is converted into rotational kinetic energy. The moment of inertia of a uniform rod about an axis through its end is $I = \dfrac{ML^2}{3}$.

Gain in rotational kinetic energy:
$\Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{ML^2}{3}\right)\omega^2$

By conservation of mechanical energy:
$Mg\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{ML^2}{3}\right)\omega^2$
$MgL = \dfrac{ML^2}{3}\omega^2$
$\omega^2 = \dfrac{3g}{L}$
$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{3g}{L}}$

Assuming the center of mass falls by $L$ incorrectly gives $\sqrt{\dfrac{6g}{L}}$, and using the moment of inertia about the center ($\dfrac{ML^2}{12}$) incorrectly gives $\sqrt{\dfrac{12g}{L}}$.

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{3g}{L}}$
